utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you as well. I, again, would like to come back to where your shells would fall. You indicated where the front lines were. Were ever shells fired from your side that went beyond the front lines and go into the rear of the enemy positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that personally I never fired a shell because I wouldn't know how to do it. We didn't shell any civilian targets because we didn't have enough shells. We would only preserve the ammunition to have it for terrible situations to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am not asking about civilian targets. I am just asking on whether shells were fired also beyond what you knew to be the confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: Well, I am not sure whether they would fall behind or in front because obviously I couldn't see, I couldn't observe. Combat zone, there is shooting. Who would watch where the shells were landing? There were some targets that we have marked of the lines and most probably it fell on the lines. Possibly, one or two may have gone over the line. Perhaps it was a higher more concentrated charge. So it would go over the line. So you wouldn't know exactly where they would fall. We would have lines that were marked; there was a scheme. It is possible that the air current as such would carry them further. Of course, there are experts who would know how to do it, and this is not my area of expertise, so I can't really answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never involved yourself in firing mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever fire a mortar in your life, I mean, apart from this conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: No. My very first time was to see infantry weapons because by establishment standards, I was always in the rear. In the JNA, I was in the kitchens. I liked to eat well, so that is where I always wanted to be. In the rear, in the kitchen. Perhaps it is funny, but that is where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. You said in the beginning you had difficulty in knowing what was a 120-millimetre shell and what was a 60-millimetre, an 82-millimetre, but slowly you -- when your experience grew, you were able to tell. Could you tell us exactly on the basis of what, what kind of experience was it that you would be better able to identify the calibre of the shell in the later stages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, this happened during experience. It happened when the shells arrived, then you would hear a hiss. It would be stronger, more intense. A hiss would be stronger. But sometimes I would be wrong. I would think that it was 120, and it turned out that it was 82. It really depended whether it would land on the asphalt, it would be a stronger impact, and a more intense echo. But it would feel on a field, then it would be less. So you would think that that was smaller shell, smaller calibre shell, but then we would know, according to our terrain, you would know where it would fall, and then you would know which one it was. Sometimes you would be wrong, but that's how we did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that on the basis of sound and on the basis of the size of the impact, you assessed the calibre of the shell. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: Yes -- no. We would assess it according to the firing. But if you listen to the shell, it has a hiss. If you hear that and you are not in the shelter, then the person would hear it without being in the shelter, that person would be dismembered. Perhaps he would survive, but it didn't happen very often. But if you hear the hiss, the whisper, so to speak, that means it would land near you. You would be up in the air and that's why we had the dugouts, the shelter. So if you would hear, you would have to run and hide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what I call "sound." Yes. You say sometimes you might be wrong. How did you know or is it just that you thought you were wrong or did you ever verify on whether your assessment was correct or not? In order to know that your assessment is wrong, you should know what is right. How did you find out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: Well, once the fighting would be over, I would go along the line and see where the shells landed and each shell has this propeller, the tail-fin, and then I would see, according to the tail-fin, I would know whether it is 120, the tail-fin is larger. And if it is a 60, it is smaller, so you know that. And then on the tail-fin, you also have a sign of the calibre. So according to the leftover, the remnant of the material, we would see which one it was. So after an attack, after the fighting and when there was a lull, then you would see whether anyone was wounded, whether anybody was killed, where the shells landed, would analyse the error of my line, whether they needed to dig ourselves further. It was important, otherwise if we made a mistake, our lives would be lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever find a tail-fin embedded in the asphalt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: No. That cannot be embedded. Only if you took a hammer and dig it in. Because once it falls, the tail-fin goes off, the whole terrain is razed as much as it was destroyed, and the only thing you have left is a crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay this answers my questions. This -- yes, Mr. Ierace and Mr. Piletta-Zanin, both. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. The questions that I need to ask are in relation to the sound and to what your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Chamber raised in relation to the sound. Further re-examination by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first question, according to your knowledge of fighting that you had, is it possible to hear a shell during its flight, that is, a mortar shell? It is possible to hear it while it is flying, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. The witness has already given evidence about that, quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the objection should be in the absence of the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask to -- for the opportunity to say something in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to clarify one thing. You told us about the hiss -- I would say more or less the hissing sound -- yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I would seek to address the Trial Chamber in the absence of the witness on a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it is a different issue. Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. There is another issue that we have to discuss, so if you would have the patience and leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope it is not very long because I am longing to go home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, while you and Your Honors were conferring, Madam Pilipovic spoke, I could not hear the words. If they were caught by tape, I would like to know what they were. If I could hear them, the witness could hear them. I think I know what one of the words was, but I would be grateful if it was caught by tape so that we can hear what they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are now here not in an adult court, but in the court of the school. I practically didn't hear what Ms. Pilipovic wanted to say to me. You are closer to Mr. Ierace. Did you hear anything, you, Mr. President, who had one ear free?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, what is it what you said so that we can get a first impression of whether it could have -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I didn't say anything to my colleague. I just turned myself because I was called by the General, and I think I said something like "it's not that" or something like that. I can't quite remember at this moment. I certainly didn't say anything in relation to what the witness could hear or register. I have no objection to have -- to listen to the tape. The tape is listened to. But I think that's what I said, something to the General, I believe, something like very quietly, it was something in relation to whether the Witness had answered the question or something to do with the sound. But as far as I remember, I didn't actually say anything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that you think you said something like "it's not that." If a witness -- if a question is put to a witness, and I think we discussed this issue before, that the line like "it's not that" let's just assume that you said something like that, could be -- it could be totally inappropriate. I ordered the Defence before not to speak at a volume that could be heard -- I do not say "was heard" but "could be heard" by the witness anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we were only commenting on whether the witness has answered that question or not. At this very moment, I really cannot rewind and I have no objection to it being listened to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why will see whether it is necessary to further investigate. But commenting or using a line such as you indicated you might have spoken, are not allowed. It is not the first time that I have to draw the attention of the Defence to that. If you want to confer, I would say just as the Judges do, if you ever overheard what we said, I would like to know, but we are usually able to speak to each other in a way that you could not hear it, and that is how it should be. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Absolutely. I am aware of that, but the only thing I can say is that it is almost impossible to have -- in communication for us to be absolutely cautious. I am trying not to communicate too loudly, but there are certain moments when things just get out of control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you should keep it under control. Mr. Ierace, what you think you heard, would that coincide with the information the Chamber just received?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I heard "no, no" followed by -- "na, na," I should say followed by some other words. At that stage, Mr. Piletta-Zanin then may a physical gesture indicating to my interpretation for Ms. Pilipovic to keep her voice down. It came in the context of the question asked to the witness requiring specifically a "yes or no" answer. Whatever the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether this what just has been said by the Defence finds confirmation in what you think you noticed. I think the matter has been dealt with now, and I would say that it should not happen again. That's the only thing that I would like to say. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to slight things, perhaps, even one thing: Sometimes we hear what you say, however, the courtesy -- but you have to know for the future, sometimes your microphone is on and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...matter had been dealt with sufficiently, that means that we could now continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to verify because we were stuck on an objection, more or less, and you've got one second --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us in one of your earlier answers: "If you listen to the shell, it has a hiss," that's how I understood your testimony. What is that hiss? Is that the sound when it flies or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hiss you can hear when the shell approaches you. At that time, it goes "Shhh," and unless the very same second you don't throw yourself into the shelter, 10, 20 metres around you, the shell has landed, and particularly if it is a 120-millimetre metre, it is a catastrophe. As soon as you hear the shell going "Shhh," you have to go into the shelter, because that means it is arriving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the sound of the shell arriving in the air to its target, is that what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question has been answered, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I just wanted clarification of what the exact answer was in order to avoid any misunderstanding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second question in relation to this that I was going to ask at a different moment at the flight of the mortar shell, before it arrives at the target, can you hear anything, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Leading in the extreme and not -- ineffectively revisits the issue which you just clarified. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think it is exactly the same. The question now is: If a mortar shell would not specifically approach you, but perhaps fly from I don't know where to I don't know where, could you then hear it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. At that time you don't hear anything, you don't see anything. When it approaches you, then it has a hiss. Because that's when it is about to land and you can hear the tail-fins hissing, going around, but somewhere up in the space, in the air, you cannot hear it because it is too far away. How could you hear it then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you can't hear it; you can't see it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, it cannot be seen, it cannot be heard. It would be like asking me, can you see a mosquito at 300 metres, of course you cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have seen it hundreds of times. It is the experience. If I would see a shell, we would have to immediately go. If you -- if you would be -- if you were able to see a shell approaching and arriving and hearing it, then nobody would ever be killed because you could hear it and see it approaching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you just told us that you couldn't see and you couldn't hear a shell if it was flying over. So would it not be difficult to establish that? Because if you do not hear or do not see anything, there are two possibilities: One, that there is a shell flying over, but you can't hear it and you can't see it; second possibility is that there was no shell flying over you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you: When a shell is fired, it doesn't arc in the air and it goes down. This arc that it's up there in the air, you cannot see it because it a far too high. It cannot be seen. It cannot be heard because it a very far away. But when it's coming down to the target approaching you, "Shhh," then that's when it explodes. So where you are when you hear the shell hissing, unless you are already in the shelter or you are throwing yourself into the shelter, then it will explode and that's it. So whoever heard the shell and wasn't -- didn't move immediately, very few have survived that. I think that's quite logical. I don't know whether you have had any contacts with the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, any other issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just to clarify things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you tell us about this whistling sound, this hiss that the mortar shell does at the moment when it is going to hit the target. Does this rule apply to all the categories, that is the ones that your have mentioned, the 60, the 82 and the 120?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: Yes, for all of them. Because when it approaches the land, you can hear it. But some of them that is heavier, it will be sooner, but sometimes if it is a smaller calibre, then it will be later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, just in order to avoid to tell the witness that this concludes his evidence, any questions from you as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier, you told us that the hissing sound was a way for you to tell if it was a 120-millimetre shell or not. Is the noise louder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not quite what the testimony of the witness is. I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]...didn't say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...please requote the part you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked a question by the President, you were asked: "Could you tell us exactly on the basis of what, what kind of experience was it, that you would be better able to identify the calibre of the shell in the later stages?" You said: "Well, let me tell you, this happened during experience. It happened when the shells arrived that you would hear a hit. It would be stronger, more intense. A hiss would be stronger." And later -- that will do, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I know where the quote comes from. Mr. Ierace hasn't provided us with a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 47 line 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the hiss you told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that the hiss assisted you to tell if it was 120-millimetre shell, rather than a shell of a different size. What was it about the hiss that enabled you to identify the shell coming in as being 120 millimetres? Was it louder or did it have a different type of sound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP21
utterances.text: Please, listen to what I am saying. I worked in a printing company. I am very familiar with words. If I say that there was an intense hiss that a 120-millimetre shell made a louder hiss, that means it was of a larger calibre. It the sound wasn't as loud, that means it was an 82 or a 60 millimetre one. I am telling you on the basis of my personal experience. This is what I heard and what I observed. So don't maltreat me too much, because if I am here and if I am talking to you, I am telling the truth didn't come to deceive anyone. A shell which is approaching its target --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the parties -- would you please look to me. All the parties are going to put questions to you. There is no question of deceiving anyone, but sometimes we want even to know more details about what you told us, and that's what Mr. Ierace is asking you. Has the question been answered, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It certainly has, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the remaining issue is how we capture in the transcript the sound that the witness has described. It is not a constant sound. There is a quaver in it or a quiver in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am afraid this cannot really describe by words, and then of course we have the audio and video. That would certainly serve us if it becomes a critical issue. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I haven't been provided with the reference. I wasn't given the reference immediately. I think that the Prosecution should provide the reference in the transcript. It is all right now. They should provide a reference for the original cassette because in the English transcript they mention "hits" and "hiss". It should be -- we should determine whether the witness is speaking of one or two different things. Is it a hit or hiss? This should be verified in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...several occasions. I think that there is -- at this moment since we have put this question several times, it was the kind of sound, and where the witness also said it was before the impact, it was not the hit. So I think that there could be not great confusion. If it would have been the answer of the witness only once, then it might have been different then what it has been discussed two, three, or four times. This then concludes your testimony in this court, Mr. DP21. You have answered all the questions both from the parties and from the Bench. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for giving your testimony in this court. And since you told us that you would very much like to go back, I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like to thank the Trial Chamber and I want to wish all the best to our Generals. I hope they will return as soon as possible and thank you once more for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...to express your wishes as to the outcome of the proceedings going on. A safe trip home again. Would you please, Mr. Usher, escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, once again. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have been informed that on page 47, line 19 -- yes. Microphone. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I am informed and I checked it that on page 47, line 19, the word "hit" is used where this confusion that I thought might not have existed, might exist. So we will check that in the original tape. At least the parties have an opportunity to do so, and I apologise for being too quick in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not a problem. That's what I suggested as a possible source of confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, we have I think two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1786, under seal, pseudonym sheet; Exhibit D1787, map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The documents are admitted into evidence as exhibits. The pseudonym sheet under seal. Then, is the Defence ready to call its next witness? Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just two matters before we do that, Mr. President. In relation to the 65 ter summary for that witness, there was no indication that the witness would give evidence as to impact characteristic of 120-millimetre mortar shells. In relation to the next witness, the most recent 65 ter summary the Prosecution has is a letter dated the 6th of November, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I just want to say that the only thing that the Defence knows is that the future is uncertain. The witnesses can appear and depending on the nature of the cross-examination, they can say things spontaneously. We had the example of the sound; we spoke about it at length. We didn't mention it because we didn't think the witness would be called to give testimony with regard to the sound and things of that nature. And then there were the poison gases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not the issue. I think the issue of Mr. Ierace is about the impact characteristics of 120-millimetre mortar shells. And I think that there were specific questions on that issue, and I did not hear any complaint about the sound of shells and neither did I on the gases.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's so, Mr. President, and the transcript reveals where Mr. Piletta-Zanin rose to his feet, it was his first question, it was essentially the thrust of his cross-examination -- examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber prefers to have an early break, an early pause. So we will adjourn until 25 minutes to 1.00 and then we will proceed with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start with the next witness, I would first like to turn into closed session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. I did not mention your name, since protective measures are granted in respect of you. So we will not use your name, and your face will not be visible for the outside world. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, since the Trial Chamber has granted protective measures for you, the Defence and those present in the courtroom shall refer to you as DP20. But first of all I will show you a document that you will have a look at, and you should confirm whether the data on the piece of paper is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: The details are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we could now go into private session so that Mr. DP20 can provide us with some more details about himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have completed that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, you told us that in 1992 you lived in Mokro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September 1992, as someone who lived in Mokro, and given your professional experience, can you tell us if you were engaged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes, I was engaged in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which positions you were engaged at.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: I was engaged within the 1st Romanija Sarajevo Brigade. It was organised on the territorial basis. It was in the wider area of Hresa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were part of the Hresa Battalion. Could you tell us whether you personally know how long the front line was, the Hresanski Battalion front line was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: I can't say precisely. 12.000, 12.400 metres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many companies there were within the battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: There were five companies at the line. It was based on the territorial principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Defence shows you a map which shows part of the town, part of the town where the neighbourhood in which you were engaged is located, could you draw the battalion lines for us there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we should now show the witness this map. The map is 3724, and we received it from the Prosecution. It is the same map that we showed the witness who testified here before this witness, and I think it would be a good idea to show this map to him in order to make things clearer for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps for the transcript, 3724, I take it that it is 3274?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. My colleague from the Prosecution said that that was a mistake that the Prosecution made. It is not 3274, it is 3724.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am making the same mistake again and again, and that is because I think that number appears on the map. But the "P" number appearing on the map is a mistake as well, as I understand. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And will there be a "D" number, Ms. Pilipovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1789.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, to the right of you, you can have a look at the map, and if possible, could you first mark the site where Hresa is on the map. Could you take a black felt-tip and draw a circle with a black felt-tip.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you write the number "1" in the circle. Could you lower the map a bit so that we can all see it, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, could you first of all tell us where the battalion command post was located in Hresa, the command post of the Hresa battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Should I mark it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mark its site, if you know what the name was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: It was here by this place called Drumovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark it with the number "2" that's where the Hresa battalion had its command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, could you mark the positions of your 3rd company. I think you said that you belonged to the 3rd company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: The Hresa Battalion was the 3rd Battalion within the Romanija Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you mark the position of the 3rd Battalion or the Hresa Battalion, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will draw a black line, you will draw a line with a black felt-tip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, if you are bending over, we see the back of your head and not the map any more. So if you would stay at a bit of a distance. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I apologise. Could the map be moved so we can see what the...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, to make things clear, could you mark these positions the places for which the Hresa Battalion front line goes, could you tell us what these positions are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes. Lapisnica, Valik, Emerovice, and Barice. The line runs through these positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said, what you have referred to a Lapisnica, Emerovice, Barice, is this something that can be seen on the map or are you saying on the basis of your experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Well, I was there, I participated in it, so it is on the basis of my experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the line, in your opinion, begin at Kozja Cuprija or Barjak where it says 1.300, elevation 1.300?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: It is to the south of elevation 1.300 which is on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, for the sake of the transcript, you have marked the front line of the Hresa Battalion which extends to the south of Sarajevo, to the north, and it is south of the elevation 1.300, and then towards the north to Emerovice, and then towards the Barice settlement. Have I said this correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't see on my copy of the map an elevation of 1.300. That may reflect the quality of the photocopy or it may be perhaps that it is a mistake for 1.003.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.003. 1.003, that's right, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It just appears below the "O" of Sarajevo, I take it, where you find the word Barjak and then below that it is 1.003.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, when you marked the front lines of the Hresa Battalion, now that you have done that, can you tell us whether you know what the line of the BH Army was, where it was with regard to the front line of your battalion, did the BH Army have a front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you personally know how far the demarcation line was from your front line? What was the distance between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Well, the distance wasn't regular. It was between 200 to 800 metres or 1.000 metres. It depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what you personally know and with regard to the lines of your battalion, could you mark the BH Army lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark those lines and could you mark them with a black felt-tip and use a dotted line. Mark their positions with respect to your positions on the line of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, for the sake of the transcript, you used the dotted line to mark the front lines of the BH Army in relation to the front line of your battalion, and to the extent that I was able to follow you. You have marked this south of the word "Sarajevo" under elevation of 896 where it says Zecja Glava, that's where the front line starts and it runs north, it is the front line of the BH Army goes through the Emerovice and Hladivode settlements and continues towards Barice. Is what I have said correct? Is this what you have marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes. Zecja Glava, Emerovice, Alipasino Polje [as interpreted], and then further on to the south of it, Barice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned Pasino Polje that that was a position held by the BH Army. Mr. DP20, can you tell us from when you were engaged as a member of the 3rd or Hresa Battalion, you said from 1992 until when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: From 1992 until the end, until the Dayton Agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that we have a transcript problem. May I have your leave? In line 23, I do not think that the witness spoke of "Alipasino Polje." I understood something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is -- I as a matter of fact the translation said something different as well. When you referred to -- when you said something about "Polje," but what Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It wasn't a Polje. It was Pasino Brdo, rather than Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. DP20, in the area of responsibility of your battalion, you were there in 1992, 1993, and 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, who was the commander of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I address you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. Do you wish to say it in a closed session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: I would only wish to mention names in closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it would be appropriate for there to be -- I withdraw that and start again. The name of a battalion commander would not normally attract protective measures. In my respectful submission, it should be given in open session unless there is a particular reason for it which the witness could, of course, give in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the name also in the testimony of the witness who told us during the Prosecution's case -- it is not in there --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...could you explain in closed session first whether -- I mean, names as such where usually mentioned unless there are specific reasons not to tell them. But let's perhaps first turn into closed session in order to discuss whether the name should be mentioned in open or in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, could you please answer the questions to who was the commander of the Hresa Battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: It was Milan Plakalovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP20, do you personally, considering you marked the front line of the Hresa Battalion, do you have any knowledges to what weapons were used by the Hresa Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Basic weapons, since this was an infantry unit, these were automatic rifles, M-70, there was also automatic rifles, there were also machine-guns, light machine-guns -- 7.9 millimetres --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't catch every single calibre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is as far as the infantry weapons are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I heard after semi-automatic rifles -- sorry -- in relation to automatic rifles, M-70, semi-automatic 76. The interpreter said that she was not able to catch all of the calibres. Perhaps the answer could be given again and more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please ask the witness to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, could you please slowly list for us what infantry weapons were in use by your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: I will do your full answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slowly please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Automatic rifles, M-70, there were semi-automatic rifles M-56 of 7.62-millimetre calibre, then I said light machine-guns M-72 machine-guns, light machine-guns, M-53 of the 7.9 millimetre --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the voice of the interpreter waned on two occasions which I think caused some problems for the transcriber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some difficulties of the voice of the interpreter very well, because also sometimes hear it at a very low volume. So could you please repeat one by one that -- so we start with the M-70, and M-70 was what kind of a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Automatic rifle, M-70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the next.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, semi-automatic rifle, M-56 of 7.62-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we now come to the next.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Machine-gun, light machine-gun 7.62 millimetres of the M-72 type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Machine-gun and light machine-guns, 7.9 millimeters, M-53. Machine-gun and semi-automatic machine-gun, 7.62 millimeters of the M-84 type. And not very many rifles of the M-48 type were of the calibre 7.9 millimeters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, what you personally were issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Automatic rifle, M-70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period from 1992, September 1992 until August 1994, how strong was your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Well, that varied, the number of troops varied from 400 to 600, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to which units were on the BH Army side in relation to the front line of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: In front of us was the 2nd Mountain Brigade of the BH Army. And specifically in this area where I marked our positions, they had about two of their battalions there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "two of their battalions," can you tell us according to the military rules, how strong is one battalion, how many troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: That depends on the establishment of units. Each army has its own establishment. As far as I know about the BH Army establishment, their battalion would have over 1.000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean one battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes, one battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you say that opposite your battalion there were two of their battalions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes, two BH Army Battalions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For this period of time, do you have personal knowledge or whether in that area of the front line of your battalion and the BH Army Battalion, was there fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis, almost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have personal knowledge which weapons were used by the members of the BH Army Battalion with respect to your positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: I can't tell you specifically for the battalion in front of us. I can tell you in general, the BH Army what weapons they used. They used the infantry weapons and the artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP20. When you say "from infantry weapons," can you tell us from which positions from infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: From the positions as I have marked them, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, you told us now that they also used artillery positions, they fired from artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Personally, do you have knowledge which positions they used, which were the artillery positions used with respect to the positions of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: They changed, the artillery positions. For instance, the mortars, they fired from Sedrenik, from the locality of Vasin Han. The so-called Babica Kuce, the Babica houses. From various positions, those in the rear, end of the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, do you have personal information as to whether there were mortars in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which types of mortars were used in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes. We had 60-, 82-, and 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your background, education, and your occupation before the conflict started and now, in your battalion that you belonged to, were there other people, other persons who had -- who were professional soldiers with a professional military background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: No, I was the only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, when you told us that in the area of your front line of your battalion that there was fighting on a daily basis, can you tell us how populated or how many populated locations were there, settlements, in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: There were populated localities on our side. These settlements that you can see on the map that I have marked, they were evacuated, there was no civilian population there in those settlements right next to the front line, to the first line of the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that there were no civilians next to the front line, could you tell us what is the area or what was the area of responsibility of your battalion in this region in terms of the depth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Depth Glog elevation point, 1.406.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you tell us on the map Glog --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how much is that in metres or kilometers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: As the crow flies, it would be about 20 kilometers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where were the soldiers of your battalion billeted when they were on the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: They were stationed in trenches on the front line or they were in the facilities for resting, either in the abandon houses right next to the front line, or in some facilities that were made for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for a clarification. What exactly is 20 kilometres? From where to where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. 20 kilometers. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mentioned Glog, and you mentioned the number "1.406." Then the next question as it appears on our English transcript is: "Can you tell us how much is that in metres or kilometres?" We had a point at that time and not a distance. So could you please tell us what -- perhaps, first, Ms. Pilipovic clarify the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We spoke about elevation point 1.406, and we are talk about the depth of the area of responsibility of your battalion. And I told you about the -- I asked you about the depth of the area, of your area of responsibility, of your battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: That was 2 to 3 kilometers. I think about 2.600 metres, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, in the period September 1992 until August 1994, you told us that there was fighting on almost a daily basis, I believe that is what you said. Can you tell us: On the front line where you say there were trenches and the houses where the troops were billeted, was there damage on the houses near the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us more about the damages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: There was damage from bullets, but there was also some larger-scale damage from artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP20, do you personally have knowledge whether in the period from September 1992 until August 1994, were there any periods when there was more intense combat, when there was some offensive operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "on several occasions," can you tell us which side in the conflict launched offensive operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: BH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us from personal experience about some periods that you know about when offensive operations took place? We are speaking from September 1992 until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: In mid-December 1992 there was an intensive attack, as the soldiers say, on the right flank -- right wing of the battalion, from the direction of Zecja Glava, Barica towards Barjak. On that occasion, they managed to take three or four trenches. After that -- that was returned, and we established the line again as it had been. Further on, very often, I can't tell you precisely about the dates, but very often there were attacks in the direction of Zecja Glava and particularly towards the locality of Barica and towards the locality of Mrkovici. Because there the main road going through Mrkojevici, and this main road was built after the conflict started and that was the only link for the Ilidza, Vogosca, and Ilijas locality with the rest of Republika Srpska. So we thought -- we assumed that their aim was to cut this communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind that we have some documents that are in English, my co-counsel will ask the witness some questions and continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. With the assistance of the usher, I would like you to have a look at a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please assist, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure about the number that should follow, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number is D1790.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, so there is no confusion, on these documents we have numbers that we have put on our exhibit list the Defence submitted. So the numbers marked are those on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We started with an exhibit that will be, therefore, 29. Could you please distribute these exhibits to all parties.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is this an exhibit that has previously been tendered and admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I will check. I think it's 24. It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So it is D24?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will check. Very well. Ms. Pilipovic will tell you exactly what's what.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1724.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, since everyone has this document now, do you manage to read English or can you read English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if on 24th of July and at the end of July 1993, there was considerable fighting in the area lato sensu --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you not lead the witness in the way you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember July 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the end of the month of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember whether at the end of July 1993 something specific happened in terms of fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes. There was still the summer offensive was still underway, the so-called summer offensive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I suggest that we do, considering that the witness cannot read English, is that I read the first paragraph of what we see under "A," and then I can ask him questions. Do I have your leave to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it would lead the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, quite demonstrably lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. Perhaps you could read the text yourselves and I will ask questions which are not leading afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want the witness to -- do you want to confront the witness what is written here or what is your -- do you want to know from him whether this is correct or not correct or -- I mean, what is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the absence of the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we would perhaps ask the witness to leave for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We sometimes have problems with these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first ask you, are you seeking confirmation of the witness that it is correct or that you think it is not correct? What is your case in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. No, we don't want the witness to say that this is correct. That is not what we are trying to obtain. What I would like is that after one has become familiar with these facts, I would like the witness to tell us whether it is not true to say that there was even more intense fighting. There are two things we can do: The importance of the -- the level of the fighting at the time and then we could relate to the credibility of the witness, and then also to see whether it is just a partial reflection of reality. But this seems to shock the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't see there is any shock. What we see here is a report of the military activity. Do you want the witness to say that it was -- I mean, if you want to confront the witness with this, you certainly seek -- and it is not quite clear to me what you seek to achieve by putting this to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that I was clear. There are two things that I want: First of all, to see that there were not more -- there wasn't more fighting; and secondly, there was more fighting than what the UN forces wanted to note, and especially regarding the shells that fell in the Serbian part. And at the same time, we could, if we can do so, we can show many things with regard to prior testimony when it was said that there was no fighting in the zone of Sedrenik, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You want to establish the level of fighting and that this is not entirely correct or not correct at all. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps my colleague could remind me, is this a Prosecution exhibit, this particular entry that he wishes to challenge? Is it already an exhibit before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure that this is a document that has been filed by the Prosecution. But in order to remind Mr. Ierace to refresh his memory, this is not something that I can do. If it is a Prosecution document, Mr. Ierace, you should know that better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- my point is this, if the Defence says this is not already in evidence, I fail to understand why they seek to challenge it. What is the relevance of challenging an account which is not in evidence before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are two things that one must distinguish. We are not contesting the document. The document exists, and we are presenting it. What we want to contest is certain parts of the contents. I don't think we should confuse matters, the document and the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber deems that it would be appropriate first to put the questions to the witness before confronting him with the document as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a second part to my objection. The passage refers to -- I take it the relevant part of the passage that my friend is interested in refers to an attack by SRK forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to remind you of the two lines rule. I have to interrupt you at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It seems that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your objection started as two lines. Could you as brief as possible, Mr. Ierace, indicate --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. The three locations indicated in the first paragraph opposite the front line indicated by this witness. So where is the basis for this witness to give such an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for someone who deals with military facts, we know that there were trajectories for shells and we know that some can go astray and we know the distance if someone can read the map between Kobilja Glava and Sedrenik which was one of the incidents of the 24th of July, 1993. We know that this is a fairly weak distance in terms of artillery. It may be fine if you go on foot, but the artillery is not great. So I think it is the Defence's right to try and prove that some of the Prosecutions witnesses who allegedly didn't hear anything, to try and prove that they lied. Because we can see that there were at least 3.000 shells that got lost in nature. So this is an obvious manifest lie, and we hope that we can prove this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may start asking questions to the witness in respect of it, but not immediately confront him with the document. So you should ask leave, when the point has come to confront him with that. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: While he is coming in, Mr. President, it would be entirely inappropriate for the Defence to contend that a Prosecution witness has lied when that has not been fairly put to the Prosecution witness

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's refrain from words like "lies," Mr. Piletta-Zanin. When you say it is the Defence case that is not in accordance with the truth, that would certainly do. As I sometimes said before, strong words do not necessarily make strong arguments. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Willingly. Mr. President, given the need for time for the translation, I will ask a few brief questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the first question, you are a professional, a military professional. You fought in the war. In general, could you provide us with general answers regarding the general events during the war, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I am now speaking about the noise an explosion makes. When a shell, an explosive shell falls and explodes, does this produce a loud noise or a not very loud noise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: It depends on the calibre of the shell. So it depends on whether it was a large or small calibre, but it is a shrill sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about large calibre shells. Can this be heard only slightly or can it be heard very well? Is the noise a loud one, the noise of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: It is a loud noise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you hear this explosion, can it also be heard far away or only in the vicinity of where the shell fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Well, that also depends on the calibre of the shells. Some can be heard further away and others can't be heard that far away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not talking about just about mortar shells, I am talking about shells in general. These could be tank shells, mortar shells, et cetera. Thank you. Witness, I would like to go back to the issue of the summer campaign in 1993. You said it was the summer campaign. You said that a large-scale offensive had been launched. Was this -- did this offensive use artillery? Was artillery used in this offensive, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The means used by the artillery were these means used on both sides, by both sides to the north or north-east of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP20
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that we have covered the basic questions now. Given the time, I don't think it would be useful to carry on now, but I will continue to ask questions about this document later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But would you think that the moment, apart from that we might have a break, that the moment might be there to start showing the document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he doesn't understand English, Mr. President, and I don't think it would be very useful to do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from -- okay. We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's coming to the point where we will adjourn. Mr. DP20, tomorrow we will not continue with your examination because the Chamber has to do another thing tomorrow. Only after we finish that, we will continue to hear -- to examine you -- not "we" but the parties will continue to examine you as a witness. Do we have any idea, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, how much time that would approximately take? Do you think that we would finish in one day and a half or one day or...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is obvious and I can't say anything else, experience today has shown this. We were very quick with the fist witness. But I don't think that the speed of the proceedings depends on me this time, so there is nothing that I can say. There is nothing I can say and there is nothing that I want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- I can't give you no indication because it is not the Chamber which ask in ultimate control on how quick we will deal with the matter we have to deal with. But I take it perhaps not tomorrow but the day after tomorrow that we will continue to examine you. The victims and witness unit will take care that you are standby, so you should make yourself available. And we hope to see you again as soon as possible, but not tomorrow morning at 9.00. Tomorrow -- yes. Tomorrow morning at 9.00 we will start with the videolink which has been put in place and we have to deal with that first because this requires the technical facilities. So we will adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace was the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am happy for Mr. Piletta-Zanin to speak first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, as I said, I only need one minute to mention certain translation issues. We will save time if I do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the Defence be required to provide us with the dates of birth, addresses, and father's names and company positions, if appropriate, by a particular date. We only have five dates of birth left or thereabouts, and we do need a reasonable period of time to complete our inquiries before the witness is called. The date of birth and the father's name and so on assists us in that regard

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to inform my colleagues that the Defence is working on this and I expect this will take place tomorrow, or the day after tomorrow at the latest this submission will be filed, because my learned colleague mentioned this last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask you, Mr. Usher, to escorts the witness out of the courtroom so we give an opportunity to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to deal with the translation issues. May I -- could you please -- you are not allowed to speak with anyone about the testimony you give in this court and you have given in this courts. So you have to refrain from any conversations with whomever about the testimony that you are giving. Yes. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, very briefly, page 11 line 12, one sentence wasn't translated in the French transcript. Likewise, page 15 line 10 where mention is made of rape and slaughter. Page 17 and 18, this concerns the English transcript now, the witness was more precise and he spoke about shells raining down on the Serb lines, that is what he literally said. Page 24 line 8, the English and French transcript don't correspond to each other. 29, 25, translation omission. 26, 23, mistranslation, no one gave instructions, orders concerning the warehouse. It concerned guarding and not giving orders. 16, 14, line 4, large-scale destruction. This notion wasn't entered -- this idea wasn't entered into the French transcript. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00, and we will then continue with the videolink.
